antennology
— A speculative discipline whose object is the shape, placement, biography, and cultural situation of antennas.

silhouette
— Primary unit of description. The register is non-functional; not pattern, gain or bandwidth, but form.

electromagnetic memory
— The permanent component of a system's state following a finite radiation pulse. A consequence, not a metaphor.

specimen
— An entry in the register, understood here as a cultural object. Its electrical function is a subsidiary fact.

directivity
The patterned distribution of an antenna's sensitivity across space. Distinct from mobility. Most engineered antennae are fixed; their preferred angles are baked into geometry.

elemental media
Media not as message-relay but as material, embodied, immersive — the precondition of contemporary life. After Peters.

jim creek, oso, washington — wartime antennae sunk into the valley to reach submarines.

The decisive difference between biological and engineered antennae is not direction but directivity: the patterned distribution of sensitivity across space. A moth scans, aligning to a chemical gradient. A Yagi-Uda antenna does not move. Its preferred angles are baked into geometry. To install one is to make a permanent claim about where signal lives.

Connected to a transceiver, an antenna can transmit and receive on the same frequency — through other antennae of the same species. The function refers to itself: filtration, materiality, conductivity, applied recursively from a ground station, through one continent to the next, all the way to the rig aboard the International Space Station. An operative chain extending from human to element to cosmos.

The exposition should be understood not as an explanation of finished works but as a continuation of their operations by other means. Artistic research, in this context, does not mean the application of theory to art, nor the production of artworks that illustrate philosophical claims. It means arranging situations in which practice can think through materials, instruments, transmissions, simulations, failures, documents, sites, and forms of delayed perception. The apparatus is therefore both technical and epistemic. It is made of antennas, receivers, sensors, projectors, renderings, seismometers, radio links, diagrams, captions, models, and also of concepts such as field, signal, memory, ground, directivity, and latency. These are not explanatory supplements to the work. They are its modes of articulation. The practice thinks when a receiver fails to coincide with a transmission, when a signal becomes briefly audible and withdraws again, when a simulation offers a visible fiction of an invisible physical process, when a field of rods in the desert is apprehended not merely as sculptural form but as an address to atmospheric electricity. In such situations, knowledge does not precede making. It is produced by staging a relation and attending carefully to what that relation allows, withholds, distorts, or transmits.

The old account of Conceptual Art often speaks of dematerialisation, as if the artwork had escaped matter into language, idea, proposition, or documentation. But the more one attends to works involving radiation, carrier waves, projected light, buried matter, atmospheric fields, or electrical systems, the less persuasive this account becomes. What appeared as dematerialisation may instead be understood as a shift in material register: from object to field, from surface to condition, from stable form to energetic implication, from perceptible matter to measurable but often inaccessible activity. A radioactive source buried in a public park is not immaterial; it is materially and energetically present in a manner that frustrates ordinary spectatorship. A carrier wave in a gallery is not immaterial; it is an electromagnetic event whose aesthetic force depends precisely on its withdrawal from unaided perception. A field of steel rods awaiting lightning is not immaterial; it is an arrangement of conductive forms, grounded potentials, meteorological anticipation, and perceptual delay. The lesson is not that the object disappeared, but that art began to operate more openly in registers where objecthood was insufficient. The artwork became harder to own, harder to see, harder to conserve, and harder to locate. It moved into duration, environment, apparatus, energy, and trust. The viewer of imperceptible art is often asked to believe, but belief here is not mystical. It is infrastructural. One believes the caption that says a radioactive source is buried somewhere nearby; one believes the instrument that registers radiation, or the receiver that converts transmission into sound, or the scientific model that describes a wave propagating across an environment. Modern perception already depends on such acts of distributed trust. We believe in radio signals we cannot feel, satellite systems we do not see, medical images generated through complex physical interactions, astronomical phenomena that arrive as data before they become pictures, and environmental measurements that exceed bodily sense. Artworks that foreground imperceptible energies do not introduce belief into an otherwise secure perceptual world. They reveal that perception has long been entangled with testimony, technical mediation, and institutional forms of credibility. The caption and the instrument become part of the aesthetic field. They do not compensate for the absence of visual evidence; they produce a different kind of encounter, one in which the viewer becomes conscious of the conditions under which something may count as present without appearing. This is why the empty photograph, the silent receiver, the dark prism, or the unstruck lightning rod may all become charged sites. They show not nothing, but the inadequacy of showing.

The desert recurs not because it is visually sublime, nor because it offers a romantic theatre of isolation, but because it sharpens the relation between signal, horizon, interference, and exposure. In the high desert, sky becomes technical condition; remoteness becomes a form of sensitivity; dryness, altitude, and distance from urban noise become part of the apparatus. The desert has long served modern art as an emblem of abstraction, reduction, and confrontation with scale. Yet it is never empty. It is crossed by weather, electromagnetic activity, geological time, military histories, radio infrastructures, speculative architectures, and artistic fantasies of pure space. To describe a desert as empty is often to describe the poverty of one's instruments. For a radio telescope, it is a site where faint cosmic signals may be gathered with less interference. For a field of lightning rods, it is a site where atmospheric charge, horizon, and anticipation can be composed. For artistic research into imperceptible energies, the desert functions as a vast, exposed receiver, a place in which the absence of conventional visual clutter does not mean the absence of activity, but the possibility of noticing other orders of activity.

Every act of reception is also an act of exclusion. To receive a signal is to contend with noise: atmospheric noise, urban noise, cosmic background, electrical interference, bodily presence, institutional distraction, semantic ambiguity, computational artefact, and the general excess of a world that cannot be fully filtered. Noise is not merely disturbance. It is the pressure of the continuous against the selectivity of the apparatus. The receiver becomes meaningful because it does not receive everything. It produces intelligibility by narrowing the field. In this sense, signal-to-noise ratio is not only a technical measure but an aesthetic and epistemological problem. What must be suppressed for something to appear? What becomes invisible or inaudible when clarity is achieved? What forms of violence, discipline, or abstraction accompany the production of a clean signal? The works here do not idealise perfect reception. Rather, they return attention to the fragile and contingent procedures through which reception happens at all. A faint sound emerging from a field of transmission, a radio image derived from cosmic emissions, a simulated waveform passing through a virtual gallery, a lightning rod waiting in a storm-prone desert: each asks how the world is filtered into experience, and what remains outside the filter.

A transmitter sends carrier waves through an exhibition space. A receiver waits, tuned and retuned, sometimes coinciding with the transmitted frequency, sometimes missing it. At unpredictable moments, a signal becomes audible. Then it withdraws again into the continuum of activity that was always present but not available to hearing. The work is not the sound alone. It is the relation between transmission and audibility, between active field and brief perceptual aperture, between the technical fact of emission and the aesthetic event of reception. This relation is crucial because it resists the reduction of art to experience. The work continues even when it is not heard. It radiates without guarantee of apprehension. Its silence is not emptiness but missed reception, or reception deferred, or reception occurring outside the body. The receiver does not simply reveal the work; it participates in making the work intermittently available. In this way, the piece produces an acoustic phenomenology of absence without becoming metaphorical. It asks the listener to attend to what exceeds listening, to imagine the gallery as crossed by organised energies whose perceptual arrival depends on tuning, timing, and coincidence.

There is a precise beauty in the moment when transmitter and receiver meet. It is not the beauty of expression, nor the beauty of form in the classical sense, but the beauty of conjugation: a technical and temporal alignment through which an otherwise inaccessible event enters the sensorium. For a moment, frequency, apparatus, space, and listener coincide. The sound appears as if from nowhere, although it has not come from nowhere. It has come from a field of prior activity whose presence was real but unavailable. Then the alignment breaks. The sound disappears, though the conditions of its disappearance are as significant as the conditions of its emergence. Such moments teach a different model of aesthetic experience. Experience is not continuous possession. It is intermittent access. The artwork is not identical with what the viewer hears, sees, or understands, but with the larger operational structure from which those moments are drawn. One might say that the work becomes perceptible only in fragments, but this would still privilege perception too much. More accurately, perception becomes one fragment of the work.

A carrier wave may carry information, music, voice, data, noise, or command. But what happens when the signal begins to fold back toward the condition of transmission itself? An electromagnetic self-portrait is not a picture of an artist, nor an image of a device, nor even a representation of a wave. It is an arrangement in which the medium indicates its own activity. The portrait is no longer resemblance but modulation. Such a gesture belongs to a lineage of reflexive practices, but it also departs from them because its reflexivity is not primarily visual, linguistic, or institutional. It is energetic and technical. The work does not say "this is art" or "this is a transmitter" in the manner of Conceptual Art's linguistic propositions. It performs the relation by which transmission becomes available to reception. In doing so, it raises a more general question: can an artwork portray the conditions that allow it to exist? Not by illustrating them, but by making those conditions operational, unstable, and perceptually contingent? The self-portrait becomes less the image of a subject than the temporary exposure of a circuit.

A virtual model of an exhibition space can begin as substitute, but it need not remain one. When physical installation becomes impossible, when travel fails, when a pandemic closes rooms, when the intended site is available only through plans, measurements, photographs, and memory, the model becomes a site in its own right. It is not simply a lesser version of an absent gallery. It is an architectural proposition constructed from distance, a technical fiction that preserves some relations while inventing others. In such a model, devices may be arranged, signals visualised, cables extended, lights added, landscapes displaced, and relations staged that would otherwise remain unrealised. The absent exhibition becomes both loss and method. This is significant for artistic research because it refuses the hierarchy in which physical installation is real and simulation is secondary. Both are constructed environments. Both require conventions of access. Both can stage invisible forces only through apparatus. The virtual installation makes this explicit. It shows that the site of the work is not identical with physical location, but with the set of relations through which perception, model, infrastructure, and imagination are brought into operative contact.

In the virtual installation, the found object returns as data. A transmitter, receiver, server rack, cable, lamp, architectural fragment, or generic technical device may arrive as a stock model: authored elsewhere, circulated through platforms, stripped of context, and made available for recombination. The readymade has become downloadable, but it has not become neutral. Stock models carry assumptions about function, realism, scale, interface, technological culture, and the generic appearance of infrastructure. They are already miniature ideologies of use. To place them in an artistic work is not merely to populate a scene. It is to work with the sedimented visual language of technical environments. The stock model is both convenient and symptomatic. It offers a ready-made image of apparatus at precisely the moment when apparatus itself is under interrogation. Treated carefully, it can become a computational cousin of the found object, not because it is physically displaced from everyday life into art, but because it is conceptually displaced from functional depiction into speculative infrastructure. It asks what kind of world has already been modelled for us, and how those models condition our sense of what technical reality looks like.

The sine wave is one of modernity's quiet emblems. It is mathematical, electrical, acoustic, visual, pedagogical, decorative, and infrastructural. It describes oscillation, but it also disciplines it, rendering fluctuation as elegance and periodicity as form. In the works considered here, the sine wave functions as a bridge between registers: sound, colour, signal, model, and transmission. A frequency may be sounded, coloured, transmitted, calculated, displayed, or imagined. Yet these registers are not equivalent. Translation between them is productive precisely because it is imperfect. When a waveform becomes sound, something is gained and something is betrayed. When frequency becomes colour, analogy risks becoming false equivalence. When a signal becomes animation, mathematical relation becomes retinal event. The point is not to claim that sound, colour, and radio frequency are the same, but to explore how technical culture routinely converts between domains in order to produce experience. The sine wave becomes a figure for that conversion: a shared contour across incompatible senses and scales.

What began as a conceptual gesture ends as an ontological provocation: a negligible quantity of radioactivity, withdrawn from view, initiates an event that does not cease. The work persists as a modification of an energetic field — a measurable perturbation that outruns exhibition, documentation, and ordinary human perception.

An apparatus is often imagined as a discrete object: a device with an input, output, housing, and function. But in these works, apparatus expands into atmosphere. A transmitter alters the status of a room; a receiver changes what silence means; a projection thickens air; a simulation turns architecture into model; a seismometer links terrestrial movement to cosmic address; a radio signal leaving orbit makes the boundary of the work difficult to name. Apparatus becomes distributed across site, device, field, and interpretation. This expansion is not merely technical. It changes the ontology of the artwork. The work is no longer a bounded object encountered by a viewer, but a condition of possible reception distributed among instruments, energies, environments, and temporalities. Such a condition may include visible components, but its decisive operations are often elsewhere. They occur in tuning, conversion, propagation, modelling, grounding, delay, and decay. To move from apparatus to atmosphere is to recognise that the work cannot be fully separated from the medium through which it acts. The medium is not a channel added after the fact. It is part of the work's body, if body remains the right word.

The seismometer listens to movements that may be too small, too distant, or too differently scaled for the body. It translates terrestrial instability into data, and in doing so redistributes authorship. The artist does not produce the signal alone. The Earth moves; the instrument measures; the system converts; the transmitter sends; the wave travels; the receiving possibility remains open. This is not collaboration with nature in a romantic sense. It is a technical compact with planetary movement. The work arises from arranging the conditions under which an environmental event can become signal, and under which signal can become artistic proposition. Such redistribution of authorship is important because it shifts attention away from expressive intention and toward operative chains. The artist becomes less origin than organiser of relays. The seismometer is not a neutral tool but a participant in the production of form. It registers according to its own capacities and limitations, producing an account of Earth that is already selective, already formatted. To treat the seismometer as author is not to personify the device, but to acknowledge that the work's agency is distributed across technical and terrestrial processes.

Messages sent into space often invite fantasies of extraterrestrial reception, as if the meaning of transmission depended on eventual recognition by another intelligence. But reception by aliens is not required for a planetary address to matter. The address is planetary before it is interstellar. It says that Earth can be technically exteriorised, that its movements can be modulated into radio, that its cultural practices can take the form of outward-travelling waves. This is not a postcard to elsewhere. It is Earth becoming signal. The distinction is important because it shifts the work away from communication understood as message delivery and toward communication understood as energetic relation. A signal may matter even if no one receives it, just as a field may operate without spectacle, and radiation may persist without spectators. The planetary address is therefore not primarily semantic. It is ontological and aesthetic. It marks the possibility that art can occur as an outward modification of a field, as an event whose scale exceeds the conditions of exhibition, and whose addressee may remain structurally uncertain.

A page receives ink. A photographic plate receives light. A wall receives projection. A magnetic drive receives difference. These familiar models encourage us to imagine inscription as something that happens on or in a substrate. But energetic memory suggests another possibility: inscription without surface, or at least without surface as the dominant figure. A trace may be distributed, residual, environmental, field-like, or detectable only through the consequences it leaves in a system. It may not resemble a mark. It may not be locatable as an object. It may persist as altered relation. This has consequences for art. Documentation can no longer be understood only as the preservation of what appeared. Conservation can no longer mean only the care of material components. Interpretation can no longer restrict itself to visible form or stated concept. Works that operate through imperceptible energies require an expanded account of trace, one that includes decay, propagation, disturbance, modulation, and the possibility of effects that exceed both spectatorship and archive. The question is not simply where the mark is. The question is what kind of world can keep it, and by what apparatuses such keeping becomes knowable.

How does one conserve a work that is not primarily an object? One may preserve diagrams, technical specifications, code, devices, installation views, captions, models, recordings, correspondence, and written accounts. These are necessary, but they do not exhaust the work. In field-based or energy-based practices, the work may also reside in relations: between transmitter and receiver, rod and storm, ground and charge, seismometer and Earth, carrier and modulation, simulation and mathematical model, signal and possible reception. Conservation becomes less like preserving an artefact and more like maintaining, describing, or reactivating conditions. Yet not all conditions can be reactivated. A transmission that has already departed cannot be retrieved as the same event. A radioactive decay curve cannot be reset without changing the work's ontology. A missed reception cannot be restored as if it had occurred. Field-like conservation must therefore include irreversibility. It must attend not only to what can be repeated, but to what has entered the world and cannot be called back. This gives such works their strange temporal force. They are not simply documented after the fact. They continue as altered conditions, as residues of operations, as remembered energies.

The antenna should not be reduced to metaphor, although it inevitably attracts metaphorical thought. It is too exact for metaphor alone. An antenna receives, transmits, resonates, filters, converts, and distributes. Its form is shaped by wavelength, frequency, conductivity, impedance, directionality, gain, environment, and purpose. It belongs simultaneously to biology, engineering, communication, warfare, astronomy, domestic technology, ecology, and art. Biological antennae extend the body into chemical, tactile, and vibrational environments; engineered antennae extend technical systems into electromagnetic space. In both cases, sensing is not merely a mental or optical act but a morphological arrangement. To become sensitive, a body or device must take shape in relation to what it seeks to detect. This is why antennae matter philosophically. They materialise relation. They demonstrate that reception is never passive and that transmission is never pure departure. An antenna does not simply open itself to the world. It selects, shapes, privileges, excludes, and transforms. It is a form of attention made material. To think with antennae is therefore to think of art not as an object offered to perception, but as an apparatus configured for relation with forces that exceed unaided sense.

Matter is often granted memory. It bears marks, scars, inscriptions, residues, ruins, sediments, and archives. Energy is more often imagined as passing: a flash, a pulse, a transmission, a charge, an event that leaves only secondary effects. Yet this division is philosophically insufficient. Energetic events alter systems. Radiation persists through decay. Electromagnetic pulses can leave residual differences. Fields can be modified. A wave can pass and still leave the world otherwise. To say that energy remembers is not to anthropomorphise energy, nor to claim that it remembers as minds or archives do. It is to insist that memory must be thought beyond the familiar forms of inscription on stable substrates. There are differences that continue, traces that are field-like rather than objectual, afterlives that cannot be reduced to documentation. This is the speculative horizon of the exposition: not the invisible as absence, not the imperceptible as lack, not energy as mere carrier, but energy as participant in the persistence of events. Such a horizon changes how artworks involving radiation, transmission, lightning, projection, simulation, and radio propagation may be understood. They do not simply pass through the world. They may leave it minutely, measurably, conceptually, or irreversibly altered.

The electromagnetic memory effect designates a permanent change induced by a finite radiation pulse — a residual kick to charged test bodies after the wave has passed. An energetic event that leaves a difference that continues. Not speculative: an entailment of the theory.

On the Plains of San Agustín, twenty-seven dish antennas — each twenty-five metres across — sit on tracks that let them be reconfigured from compact to thirty-nine kilometres apart. Each dish receives radio frequency from space. The signals from all dishes are then combined through a process of interference: the image is not captured in a single optical instant but synthesised from signals gathered across a maximum baseline of thirty-nine kilometres and correlated through computation. Baseline spacing is the instrument. The resolution of the VLA is determined not by the diameter of any individual dish but by the distance between them. The array sees by separating. What no single element could discern, the distributed system synthesises from the differential arrival of the same wavefront at different points in space. Earth is not incidental to this apparatus. As the planet rotates, the geometry of the array shifts, the effective aperture grows, and the planet itself becomes a component of the synthetic lens. The VLA does not magnify; it correlates. Its resolution is a function of separation, not accumulation.

A grid of polished steel rods in the New Mexico desert can be seen as sculpture, drawing, architecture, meteorological instrument, or philosophical proposition. Its rods stand in measured intervals, their tips aligned to produce a horizontal plane across uneven land. In ordinary conditions, they catch and reflect light; at certain times they almost disappear; under storm conditions they become charged with the possibility of conducting lightning. The work is famous for an event that most visitors will not see. This is essential. Its aesthetic power is not reducible to the spectacle of a strike, but to the durational arrangement of expectation: the waiting, the horizon, the knowledge of possible discharge, the conversion of landscape into field. The work stages reception as potential. It allows the viewer to inhabit a relation between geometric precision and atmospheric contingency. Its rods do not simply occupy the desert; they tune it. They mark the land as a place where electricity may pass, where sky and ground might briefly enter visible violence, where sculpture becomes less a fixed object than a prepared relation to an energetic event. Lightning need not appear for the work to operate. The poles are already grounded; the circuit is already closed. What lightning adds is not reception but visibility of what was always occurring. The possibility of reception is already part of reception.

Antennae appeared first as biological appendages — extending the membrane of an animate body into its environment. Insect and crustacean antennae translate chemical, mechanical, and electromagnetic signals into electrical impulses a nervous system can read. Engineered antennae arrived later, doing the same work in metal: Maxwell's equations made into a rod. Form follows wavelength. The lengths and diameters of antennae are tuned to fractions of the waves they receive. The fan of a Rhipicera beetle maps the gradient of a pheromone; the parabola of a radio telescope focuses cosmic signal onto a receiver suspended at its focus. In biology and in engineering, the same constraint operates — proportion to the unseen.
Energy, too, remembers.
Antennae are doors — but doors opening to a cosmos devoid of an outdoors.
Art as radar acts as an early alarm system, enabling us to discover social and psychic targets in lots of time to prepare to cope with them.
twelve of two thousand four hundred sixty-three —
objects that need not exist to be thought
the return stroke travels skyward — what we see is the answer, not the call
the male silk moth is tuned to a single frequency — pheromone
